_export_meta.target_lesson_title: Physical Indicators of Health & Interpreting Data
_export_meta.adaptation_notes: BTEC Tech Award Component 3 teaches BMI, blood pressure, peak flow and resting pulse rate with very similar emphasis on reading values against published guidelines — close conceptual overlap. The BTEC build uses NHS BMI categories and published BP ranges as worked examples; that pedagogy transfers directly. Adapt by adding waist-to-hip ratio (additional indicator in this spec, not in BTEC) and the four named contributing factors (age, sex, lifestyle, environment). Reframe BTEC's care-plan focus to this spec's data-interpretation focus — students here are asked to read a stimulus table, not write a care plan.

source_lesson.title: Environmental Factors & Life Events
source_lesson.description: How housing, pollution, and major life events affect physical and emotional wellbeing.
source_lesson.content_html:
Environmental Factors

The environment in which a person lives, works, and spends their time has a direct effect on their health and wellbeing. Environmental factors include housing conditions, the home environment, and exposure to different types of pollution. Unlike lifestyle factors, individuals may have limited control over their environment — especially if they are affected by poverty or live in a deprived area.

Housing

The specification identifies three aspects of housing: housing needs, housing conditions, and housing location.

Housing needs relate to whether a home is suitable for the people living in it. An elderly person needs a home without stairs or with a stairlift. A family with young children needs enough bedrooms and a safe outdoor space. Overcrowding occurs when there are too many people for the size of the property, leading to stress, lack of privacy, poor sleep, and increased spread of infections.

Housing conditions refer to the state of the property itself. Damp, cold, and poorly maintained homes increase the risk of respiratory conditions like asthma, cause joint pain, and create an unpleasant living environment. Mould growth in damp homes can trigger allergies and breathing problems. Poor housing conditions are strongly linked to anxiety, depression, and low self-esteem because the individual feels they have no control over their living situation.

Key Fact

Poor housing conditions (damp, cold, overcrowding) negatively affect physical health (respiratory problems, infections), emotional wellbeing (stress, anxiety, low self-esteem), and social wellbeing (embarrassment about inviting people home, lack of private space).

Housing location affects access to services, employment, education, and social opportunities. Living in a rural area may mean long distances to hospitals, shops, and schools, leading to social isolation. Living in an area with high crime rates can cause fear and anxiety. Conversely, living in a safe neighbourhood with good transport links, parks, and community facilities supports positive health and wellbeing.

Home Environment

The home environment refers to the atmosphere within the home — not just the physical building but the relationships, routines, and emotional climate. A warm, clean, safe, and loving home environment supports positive development across all PIES areas. A chaotic, dirty, unsafe, or hostile home environment has the opposite effect.

For example, a child growing up in a home where there is domestic violence will experience fear, anxiety, and insecurity (emotional), difficulty concentrating at school (intellectual), potential physical harm (physical), and difficulty forming healthy relationships (social). The home environment is particularly important for children and young people, as it shapes their development during critical life stages.

Exposure to Pollution

The specification identifies three types of pollution that affect health and wellbeing.

Air pollution: Caused by traffic fumes, industrial emissions, and burning fossil fuels. It worsens respiratory conditions like asthma and COPD, increases the risk of lung cancer and cardiovascular disease, and can cause headaches and fatigue. People living near busy roads or in cities are most affected.

Noise pollution: Caused by traffic, construction, aircraft, and loud neighbours. Prolonged exposure to noise can cause hearing damage, sleep disturbance, increased stress and anxiety, difficulty concentrating, raised blood pressure, and irritability. It particularly affects emotional and intellectual wellbeing.

Light pollution: Caused by excessive artificial lighting from street lights, buildings, and screens. It disrupts sleep patterns by interfering with the body’s natural circadian rhythm (sleep-wake cycle). Poor sleep leads to fatigue, reduced concentration, weakened immunity, and increased stress. Screen use before bed is a common cause of light pollution affecting young people.

Life Events

A life event is a significant event or change that affects a person’s development. Life events can be expected (planned, like retirement) or unexpected (unplanned, like an accident). The specification groups life events into three categories and requires you to understand how they impact PIES development.

Key Fact

Life events are grouped into three categories: physical events (accident/injury, physical illness, mental and emotional health), relationship changes (marriage, divorce, parenthood, bereavement), and life circumstances (moving house/school/job, redundancy, imprisonment, retirement).

Physical Events

Accident or injury can cause pain, disability, and loss of independence (physical), difficulty concentrating or returning to work or education (intellectual), fear, frustration, and anxiety about recovery (emotional), and social isolation if mobility is reduced (social). Physical illness has similar effects — a serious diagnosis like cancer affects every area of PIES. Mental and emotional health events such as developing depression or experiencing a breakdown affect the ability to function in daily life, maintain relationships, and engage with education or work.

Relationship Changes

Marriage or civil partnership can positively affect wellbeing by providing emotional security, companionship, and shared financial resources. However, it can also bring stress if the relationship is difficult. Divorce or separation can cause grief, loss of income, disruption to children’s lives, loss of shared friendships, and reduced self-esteem. Parenthood brings joy and purpose but also exhaustion, financial pressure, and reduced social life. Bereavement — the death of a loved one — causes grief, loneliness, and can trigger depression. It affects all PIES areas and the impact can last months or years.

Moving house, school, or job can be exciting but also stressful — it disrupts routines, removes familiar social networks, and requires adaptation to new environments. Children who move schools frequently may struggle academically and socially. Exclusion from education removes access to learning, peer relationships, and routine. Redundancy causes loss of income, purpose, and social contact. Imprisonment separates the individual from family and community, causes stigma, and limits future employment. Retirement provides freedom from work pressure but can lead to loss of purpose, reduced social contact, and financial anxiety if income drops.

The impact of any life event depends on the individual’s resilience, the support available to them, and their personal circumstances. Two people experiencing the same life event may respond very differently.
source_lesson.exam_tip_html: When discussing life events in the exam, always consider the individual’s life stage (Component 1). A bereavement affects a child differently from an adult. Redundancy impacts someone in early adulthood (career-building stage) differently from someone in later adulthood (near retirement). Making these synoptic links to other components earns higher marks.
source_lesson.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Environmental factors (housing needs/conditions/location, home environment, air/noise/light pollution) directly affect physical health and emotional wellbeing, often beyond the individual’s control.
  • Life events fall into three categories: physical events, relationship changes, and life circumstances — each can have positive and negative effects across PIES.
  • The impact of life events depends on the individual’s resilience, available support, and personal circumstances.

practice_questions.text: Identify one type of pollution that can affect an individual's health and wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark(s) for one correct identification:
• Air pollution (1)
• Noise pollution (1)
• Light pollution (1).

practice_questions.text: Give two ways that poor housing conditions can negatively affect an individual's health and wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks:
1 marks for each correct way (max 2):
• Damp causes respiratory problems/asthma (1)
• Cold homes cause joint pain (1)
• Mould triggers allergies (1)
• Overcrowding causes stress/poor sleep (1)
• Poor conditions cause anxiety/low self-esteem (1)
• Embarrassment prevents inviting people home (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how bereavement can affect an individual's emotional and social wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks for developed explanation:
• Emotionally, bereavement causes grief and sadness (1) because the individual has lost someone important to them, which can lead to depression and difficulty coping with daily life (1).
• Socially, bereavement can cause loneliness and isolation (1) because the individual may withdraw from social activities or lose the companionship that the deceased person provided (1).
• Accept other valid chains of reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Discuss how environmental factors can affect an individual's health and wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Detailed discussion covering multiple environmental factors and PIES areas.
Mid band (3-4): Some discussion with partial development.
Lower band (1-2): Limited points with little development.
Indicative content:
• Housing conditions: damp and cold increase respiratory problems; overcrowding causes stress
• Housing location: rural areas reduce access to services; high crime areas cause anxiety
• Home environment: domestic violence affects all PIES; loving home supports development
• Air pollution: worsens asthma and COPD, increases CVD risk
• Noise pollution: disrupts sleep, increases stress, damages hearing
• Light pollution: disrupts sleep patterns, reduces concentration
• Links between factors: poor housing often linked to poverty (economic factor).

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the extent to which expected life events have a more positive impact on health and wellbeing than unexpected life events.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Comprehensive evaluation with balanced argument and justified conclusion.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Good evaluation with some balance.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some evaluation with limited balance.
Lower band (1-2): Limited evaluation.
Indicative content:
Expected life events:
• Planned for, so individual can prepare — e.g. saving money before retirement
• Marriage/parenthood bring joy, purpose, emotional security
• Moving house by choice can improve living conditions
• However, even expected events cause stress — parenthood brings exhaustion, retirement causes loss of purpose
Unexpected life events:
• No time to prepare — can be traumatic (e.g. accident, redundancy)
• Bereavement causes grief and can lead to depression
• Sudden illness disrupts all areas of life
• However, some unexpected events can be positive — an unexpected job offer
Conclusion: Expected events generally allow more preparation and control, which can reduce negative impacts. However, the actual effect depends on the nature of the event, the individual's resilience, and the support available. Both types can have positive and negative impacts.

practice_questions.text: Sarah is 72 years old. She lives alone in a cold, damp flat on the third floor with no lift. She recently lost her husband and has been feeling very lonely. Her nearest family live 40 miles away. The flat is near a busy main road. Using the case study, assess how environmental factors and life events are affecting Sarah's overall health and wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (8-10): Comprehensive response covering all PIES areas with clear links to Sarah's circumstances.
Upper-mid band (5-7): Good coverage of multiple PIES areas with some links.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant points but limited development.
Lower band (1-2): Basic points with little reference to the case study.
Indicative content:
• Physical: Cold, damp flat increases risk of respiratory problems and joint pain — particularly harmful for a 72-year-old. Third floor with no lift limits mobility and may prevent her going out. Air pollution from busy road worsens respiratory conditions.
• Intellectual: Loneliness and isolation reduce mental stimulation. Lack of social interaction may accelerate cognitive decline at her age. Noise from the road may disrupt concentration and sleep.
• Emotional: Bereavement causes grief, sadness, and loneliness. Living alone after losing her husband removes emotional support. Poor housing conditions create anxiety and helplessness. She is in later adulthood where emotional wellbeing is linked to attachment and security.
• Social: Living alone with family far away limits social contact. Third floor with no lift may prevent her from going out to socialise. Loneliness is a major risk factor for poor health in later adulthood.
• Links: Environmental factors (housing) compound the life event (bereavement). Her age and life stage (later adulthood) make her more vulnerable. Multiple factors interact — isolation worsens grief, poor housing worsens physical and emotional health.
• Synoptic: In later adulthood, physical decline is expected (Component 1). Health and social care services could provide support (Component 2) — housing adaptations, bereavement counselling, social groups.

glossary_terms.definition: The physical surroundings and conditions in which a person lives, including housing, home environment, and exposure to pollution.
The atmosphere and conditions within a person’s home, including cleanliness, safety, warmth, and the relationships between household members.
A significant event or change in a person’s life that can affect their physical, intellectual, emotional, and social development.
The ability to recover quickly from difficulties and adapt to change.
